frontmatter_description: Diagnose the means-end structure among a character's goals: which goal is the end, which is a subgoal or local step serving it.
title: Goal Hierarchy
use_when: Use when one stated goal is an instrument or step taken in order to reach another goal, and you must say which is the end and which is the means.
Use when a character does a small task only because it unlocks something they wanted all along (e.g., helps a neighbor to earn money, then uses the money for their original aim).
Use when the question is about the level or nesting of goals (long-term aim vs. short-term step vs. local action), not about which of two rival goals the character picks.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when two goals COMPETE and the question is which one wins or is weighted higher with no nesting between them; that is free weighing of rival goals (Goal-Conflict Arbitration, micro-25).
Do not use when a binding prior promise, ongoing task, or schedule decides what gets done first; that is Commitment Priority (micro-24).
Do not use when the question asks what the character will physically do next from their goal; that is Action Prediction (micro-23).
Do not use when the issue is inferring the immediate purpose behind one present behavior; that is Intention Recognition (micro-22).
Do not use when the issue is reading what the character or another person likes or wants (self- or other-preference, micro-19/micro-20).
decision_variable: the means-end (nesting) relation among goals: which goal is superordinate (the end) and which is subordinate (a step serving it)
trigger_checklist: Two or more goals, plans, or aims are present and one is performed in order to obtain another.
You can phrase the link as 'does A so that B' or 'A is a step toward B'.
The goals do not compete for the same slot; completing the subgoal advances, not blocks, the end goal.
The question is about level/structure (end vs. step), not about which rival goal is chosen or what happens next.
workflow: List every stated goal, plan, or action and the character's original want.
For each pair, test 'is A done in order to reach B?' If yes, A is the subordinate (means) and B is the superordinate (end).
Trace the full chain to the top: the original want the character is ultimately trying to satisfy is the end goal.
Map each item as end goal, intermediate means, or local step. Answer with that structure, or with the action that shows the character resuming the END goal after a subgoal is done.

special_case.title: Detour subgoal that unlocks the original want
special_case.rule: When a character pauses an original want to do a task that supplies the means (money, permission, an item) for that same want, the task is a subordinate step; the original want is still the end goal and is resumed once the means is obtained.

worked_example.scene: Tom finds money and wants to buy things with it. An aunt offers him money if he helps pick apples, so he stays to pick apples.
worked_example.question: What does Tom do after he helps the aunt pick apples?
worked_example.answer_logic: Picking apples is a subordinate step taken only to earn money; buying things was, and remains, the superordinate end goal. So once the subgoal is done, Tom goes to spend the money on the things he wanted, not back to the aunt's chores or off to play.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to the free-weighing-of-rival-goals capability if two goals compete for the same slot and the question is which one wins or matters more (Goal-Conflict Arbitration, micro-25).
Exit to the binding-commitment capability if a prior promise, ongoing task, or schedule is what decides the order of action (Commitment Priority, micro-24).
Exit to the next-action-prediction capability if the scene asks what the character will physically do next (Action Prediction, micro-23).
Exit to the immediate-purpose-of-a-behavior capability if the issue is inferring why one current behavior is happening (Intention Recognition, micro-22).
Exit to the desire/preference-reading capability if the issue is what the character's own or another person's likes or wants are (self-preference micro-19 / other-preference micro-20).

references.route_signal: Use this unit when one goal is done in order to reach another and you must name which is the end and which is the step. If instead two goals compete with no nesting, route elsewhere.
hard_boundary: Hierarchy = means-end STRUCTURE (A serves B); not which of two competing goals wins, which is free weighing of rival goals (Goal-Conflict Arbitration, micro-25).
Hierarchy is structural level; it is not the order forced by a binding promise or schedule, which is the binding-commitment capability (Commitment Priority, micro-24).
Hierarchy is about goal level, not the immediate purpose of one present behavior, which is Intention Recognition (micro-22).
Hierarchy is goal nesting, not the next observable action, which is Action Prediction (micro-23).
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not treat the goal mentioned first, or the action happening first in time, as the higher-level goal; order in the text or timeline is not level.
Do not treat the subgoal the character is currently busy with as the main aim; the end goal is the original want it serves.
Do not collapse a means-end chain into a conflict; here the subgoal advances the end goal, it does not compete with it.
common_failure_modes: Confusing a subtask the character is doing right now with the main objective it serves.
Reading a means-end chain as a goal conflict and trying to pick a winner.
Assuming the character abandons the original want once they start the detour task, when in fact they resume it.
Equating long-term with 'more preferred' or short-term with 'less important' without textual support.

minimal_pair.case: Tom wants to buy things; an aunt offers money if he picks apples, so he picks apples first. Question: what does he do afterward?
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Picking apples is a subordinate step serving the end goal of buying things; recognizing the nesting predicts he resumes the original want. In-scope means-end structure.

minimal_pair.case: Li Hua loves outdoor adventure; Wang Fang prefers the quiet library; they must pick one place for the weekend. Question: where do they go?
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Two goals compete head-to-head with no nesting (neither serves the other), so the answer is a weighing of rival goals, not a hierarchy. Routes to the free-weighing capability (Goal-Conflict Arbitration, micro-25).

boundary_stress_test: If two goals compete for the same slot and the answer names a winner, this is weighing of rival goals, not hierarchy.
If a binding promise or schedule is what sets the order, this is the binding-commitment capability, not hierarchy.
If the story asks what the person will physically do next as the endpoint, route to action prediction even if goals are present.
If the only clue that one goal is 'higher' is that it happens earlier in time, that is not evidence of level.
references.generalization_note: Use this unit only for means-end structure among goals (which goal serves which). It does not pick a winner among competing goals, does not resolve binding commitments, and does not output the next action.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: One goal is done in order to obtain another goal (a means-end chain), and the answer turns on recognizing the subordinate step serves the superordinate end goal.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: Two goals compete head-to-head with no nesting and the question asks which one is chosen (free weighing of rival goals).
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The scene supplies goals plus social cues and asks what the character will physically do next (action prediction).

notes: This unit supports diagnosis inside broader goal-action scenes, but only for means-end structure, not selection.
Keep the answer structural: end goal, intermediate means, or local step (or the action that shows the end goal being resumed after a subgoal).
The decisive test is 'A in order to B'; if no goal serves another, this is not the right unit.
core_question: Distinguish long-term, short-term, and local goals
